Core concepts

Core concepts

The mental model behind routiva: the layer stack, next(), the raw wrappers, async errors and app settings.

The mental model#

An app is a router. A router is an ordered list of layers. A layer is a route, a piece of middleware, or an error handler. A request walks the list from top to bottom; each layer either responds, passes control with next(), or signals a failure with next(err).

text
createApp() ─▶ App (extends Router)
                 │
                 └─ stack: [ layer, layer, layer, … ]
                             │
        request ────────────▶ walk top to bottom ─▶ first response wins

App extends Router#

App is a Router with an HTTP server, settings and default responses added. From src/app.js:

js
export class App extends Router {
  constructor(options = {}) {
    super();
    this.settings = Object.create(null);
    this.set('env', options.env || process.env.NODE_ENV || 'development');
    // ...
  }
}

Every routing method — get, post, use, param, route — is defined on Router, so an app has them all. A Router on its own is the building block for modular sub-routers:

js
import { Router } from 'routiva';

const api = new Router();
api.get('/status', (req, res) => res.json({ ok: true }));

app.use('/api', api);   // mounted at a prefix

Everything is a layer#

Registering a handler pushes one object onto this.stack. A route with three handlers pushes three layers. The shape, from src/router.js:

js
this.stack.push({
  method,               // 'GET' | null (middleware / all)
  path,                 // original pattern, for debugging
  regex,                // compiled matcher, built once
  keys,                 // captured parameter names
  fn: handler,          // the function actually invoked
  owner: this,          // which Router registered it
  isMiddleware,         // prefix match vs exact match
  isErrorHandler: handler.length === 4,
});

Routes and middleware share the same array. There is no separate "middleware phase" and "route phase" — only the order you registered things in. Paths are compiled to a RegExp once, at registration, and reused for every request.

next() and next(err)#

A handler that does not respond must call next(). Calling next(err) switches the stack into error mode. dispatch() enforces the switch with one comparison (src/router.js, abridged):

js
function dispatch(stack, req, res, done) {
  let index = 0;
  let finished = false;

  function next(err) {
    if (finished) return;                                 // done() runs once
    if (index >= stack.length) { finished = true; return done(err); }
    const wantsError = Boolean(err);
    let layer, match;
    while (index < stack.length) {
      layer = stack[index++];
      if (layer.isErrorHandler !== wantsError) continue;  // 4-arity ⇔ error mode
      match = layer.regex.exec(req.path);
      if (!match) continue;
      if (!methodAllows(layer, req)) continue;            // HEAD→GET, 405
      break;
    }
    if (!match) { finished = true; return done(err); }
    invoke(layer, match, err, req, res, next);
  }

  next();
}

A shared cursor means next() from any depth walks forward through the same list without re-running earlier layers. The finished latch guarantees done runs once even if a handler calls next() twice.

Registration order is execution order#

A use() written before your routes runs first. An error handler written after your routes can catch their errors; one written before them cannot, because it has already been passed.

js
app.use(logger());                 // runs first
app.get('/users', listUsers);      // runs next
app.use((err, req, res, next) => { // runs only if a later layer calls next(err)
  res.status(err.status || 500).json({ error: { message: err.message } });
});

Error handlers are arity 4#

The only rule is the function's length. Four parameters marks an error handler; three marks an ordinary handler or middleware. No registration API is needed.

js
app.use((req, res, next) => { /* normal */ });     // length === 3
app.use((err, req, res, next) => { /* error */ });  // length === 4

If no error handler responds, App._handleError builds a JSON error. HttpError sets expose = status < 500, so 4xx messages reach the client while 5xx messages are hidden unless expose stack is on:

js
const expose = this.setting('expose stack');
const message = error.expose || expose ? error.message : statusMessage(status);
res.status(status).json({ error: { message, status } });

Request and Response are thin wrappers#

Node's IncomingMessage and ServerResponse are wrapped once per request. Both originals stay reachable as req.raw and res.raw, so the framework never hides the socket — anything the wrapper does not cover (req.raw.setTimeout, res.raw.writeHead) is still one property away.

Request parses the URL, query, cookies and client IP in its constructor, so per-request work happens once. Response makes every mutator chainable (res.status(201).type('json').send({ ok: true })) and guards against a second send by checking res.raw.headersSent || res.raw.writableEnded.

Async handlers#

Handlers may return a promise. routiva attaches .catch(next) to every returned promise (src/router.js), so a rejection is forwarded to the error chain exactly like a synchronous throw — no wrapper library needed:

js
app.get('/data', async (req, res) => {
  const row = await db.get(req.params.id);  // rejection reaches your error handler
  res.json(row);
});

This matches Express 5 behaviour. Express 4 only forwarded synchronous throws.

Settings#

App stores settings on a null-prototype object. Read them with app.setting(key), write with app.set(key, value) or the boolean helpers app.enable(key) / app.disable(key). Constructor options set the same keys up front.

SettingDefaultEffect
envprocess.env.NODE_ENV or 'development'Environment name
trust proxyfalsereq.ip / req.ips read X-Forwarded-For
x-powered-byfalseAdds X-Powered-By: routiva to responses
json spaces0Reserved
expose stackenv !== 'production'5xx messages and stack traces in error responses
js
const app = createApp({ trustProxy: true, xPoweredBy: false });
app.disable('x-powered-by');
app.set('json spaces', 2);

trust proxy also accepts a number: with n, req.ip is taken n hops from the right of X-Forwarded-For.

The request lifecycle#

text
  Client           App._handle            Router.handle          layer            Response
    │  GET /users/1 ─▶│ wrap req/res ──────▶│ dispatch(stack) ─────▶│ handler(req,res) │
    │                 │                     │                      │ res.status/json ▶│
    │◀─────────────────────── 200 application/json ─────────────────────────────────── │
    │                 │◀── done(err) ───────│ (only if nothing responded)
    │                 │  _handleError(err)  or  _handleNotFound(req, res)
  1. _handle wraps the raw request and response.
  2. Router.handle dispatches the stack, matching methods, params and prefixes.
  3. If a layer responds, the request is done.
  4. Otherwise done() produces a 404, a 405 with an Allow header, or an auto 204 for OPTIONS.
  5. If an error was raised, _handleError produces a safe JSON error instead.

Why zero dependencies#

routiva imports only Node built-ins: node:http, node:url, node:fs, node:path, node:zlib and node:crypto. That keeps the install tree at one package and the entire framework in files you can read in an afternoon. The trade-off is ecosystem size — routing, body parsing, static files, CORS, compression and rate limiting ship in the core, but template engines, sessions and third-party plugins do not.
